facts.text: The white-eared honeyeater is easy to spot thanks to its olive-green body, black head and striking white ear-patch.
facts.quote: White-eared honeyeaters are easily identifiable by their olive-green body, black head and white ear-patch.

facts.text: It is a medium-sized honeyeater, 19–22 centimetres in length, weighing about 20 g, and males and females look alike.
facts.quote: The white-eared honeyeater is a medium-sized honeyeater 19–22 centimetres (7.5–8.7 in) in length. There is no sexual dimorphism, with males and females looking alike. They weigh approximately 20 g (0.71 oz)

facts.text: Its call is deep and mellow, with phrases like chwok, chwok, chwok-whit and kwitchu, kwitchu.
facts.quote: Their voice is deep and mellow but slightly metallic chwok, chwok, chwok-whit and kwitchu, kwitchu; very sharply scratchy, metallic chwik!.

facts.text: Usually solitary, the white-eared honeyeater can be sedentary, nomadic or locally migratory.
facts.quote: White-eared honeyeaters are usually solitary, but may also be found in small family groups. They can be sedentary, nomadic or locally migratory.

facts.text: It plucks fur and hair from livestock, humans, kangaroos and wallabies to line its cobweb-bound cup nest.
facts.quote: White-eared honeyeaters will pluck fur and hairs from livestock, humans, and native wildlife, such as kangaroos and wallabies.

facts.text: While foraging, it searches intensively for insect prey, averaging one insect every 5 seconds.
facts.quote: While foraging, the white-eared honeyeater searches intensively for its insect prey, averaging one insect every 5 seconds.

facts.text: It eats nectar in spring and summer (August - December) but switches to insects for the rest of the year.
facts.quote: They feed on nectar during the spring and summer (August - December), but switch to insects for the rest of the year.

facts.text: Its preferred habitat is forests, woodlands, heathlands, mallee and dry inland scrublands with a eucalyptus canopy, rough bark and a shrub layer.
facts.quote: The white-eared honeyeater's preferred habitat is in forests, woodlands, heathlands, mallee and dry inland scrublands. A eucalyptus canopy, rough bark and a shrub layer are the most important requirements for white-eared honeyeaters.

facts.text: Despite a decreasing population, its extensive distribution means it is considered of least concern on the IUCN Red List.
facts.quote: Although the white-eared honeyeater has a decreasing population, it has an extensive distribution, and is considered to be of least concern on the IUCN Red List.

facts.text: The species was first described by English ornithologist John Latham in 1801 as Turdus leucotis.
facts.quote: The white-eared honeyeater was first described by English ornithologist John Latham in 1801 as Turdus leucotis.
